content: Endometrial cancer is one of the most prevalent gynecological malignancies globally, and its incidence is increasing, partly due to rising obesity rates. Endometrial hyperplasia, a precancerous condition, can progress to endometrial cancer if left untreated. This condition is more common than endometrial cancer itself. Current treatment options, such as oral progesterone tablets, are associated with adverse effects in up to 84% of women. While the levonorgestrel intrauterine device (IUD) may improve treatment adherence, it is invasive, not acceptable to all women, and causes irregular vaginal bleeding in 82% of cases. Therefore, alternative therapeutic options are necessary. Metformin, a medication commonly used to manage diabetes, has shown potential in reversing endometrial hyperplasia in some human studies. However, its efficacy and safety for this indication remain uncertain. This review aimed to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of metformin in treating women with endometrial hyperplasia. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and cross-over trials comparing metformin (alone or in combination with other therapies) to placebo, no treatment, conventional medical treatments, or other active interventions in women with histologically confirmed endometrial hyperplasia. Seven RCTs involving 387 women were included in the analysis. The primary outcome was the regression of endometrial hyperplasia (with or without atypia) to normal histology. In the comparison of metformin plus megestrol versus megestrol alone, the evidence for regression of endometrial hyperplasia was rated as low-certainty. The quality of evidence for other outcomes in all comparisons was rated as very low. Although selection bias was low, many studies had a high risk of performance and detection bias due to inadequate blinding. This review identified four new RCTs and six ongoing RCTs. When comparing metformin to megestrol, it is uncertain whether metformin increases the regression of endometrial hyperplasia to normal histology. The odds ratio (OR) was 4.89 (95% confidence interval [CI] 1.56 to 15.32; P = 0.006; 2 RCTs, 83 participants; I² = 7%; very low-certainty evidence). If the regression rate with megestrol is 61%, the regression rate with metformin would be between 71% and 96%. There is no conclusive evidence regarding differences in rates of abnormal uterine bleeding or hysterectomy between the two treatments. No studies reported on progression to endometrial cancer, recurrence of hyperplasia, health-related quality of life, or adverse effects during treatment. In the comparison of metformin plus megestrol versus megestrol monotherapy, the combination may improve regression of endometrial hyperplasia to normal histology compared to megestrol alone (OR 3.27, 95% CI 1.65 to 6.51; P = 0.0007; 4 RCTs, 258 participants; I² = 0%; low-certainty evidence). If the regression rate with megestrol alone is 54%, the rate with the addition of metformin would be between 66% and 84%. In one study, 37.5% of participants taking metformin experienced nausea, which resolved without further treatment. It remains unclear whether the combination therapy affects recurrence rates, progression to endometrial cancer, or hysterectomy rates compared to megestrol alone. No studies reported on abnormal uterine bleeding or health-related quality of life. In the comparison of metformin plus levonorgestrel IUD versus levonorgestrel IUD monotherapy, it is uncertain whether there is a difference in regression of endometrial hyperplasia to normal histology (OR 0.29, 95% CI 0.01 to 7.56; 1 RCT, 46 participants; very low-certainty evidence). If the regression rate with levonorgestrel alone is 96%, the rate with the addition of metformin would be between 73% and 100%. There is no conclusive evidence regarding differences in rates of abnormal uterine bleeding, hysterectomy, or adverse effects between the two treatments. No studies reported on recurrence of hyperplasia, progression to endometrial cancer, or health-related quality of life. In conclusion, the current evidence is insufficient to support or refute the use of metformin, either alone or in combination with standard therapies such as megestrol acetate, for the treatment of endometrial hyperplasia. Well-designed and adequately powered RCTs with long-term outcome data are needed to address this clinical question.
